# Lifecycle and Scopes

Use this page to decide how long each object lives and who stops it. In Onity a scope is an
`OnityContainer` with its children. The scope owns the services it created, the subscriptions tied to
it, the async work started with its token, and the pools it created, and it disposes them together in a
fixed order. You never write teardown code that tracks these one by one.

## One lifetime model

Every pillar attaches to the scope the same way:

- Services bound with `AsSingle()` or `AsScoped()`, and the primitives created by the binding helpers,
  are disposed by the scope when they implement `IDisposable`.
- Subscriptions are retained with `AddTo(scope)` (`Onity.DI`), which disposes them when the scope
  ends.
- Async work takes the scope token (`IOnityScopeLifetime.Token`, `OnityContainer.LifetimeToken`,
  `OnityContext.LifetimeToken` or `component.GetScopeCancellationToken()`), which is canceled when the
  scope ends.
- Pools created by `BindPooledFactory(prefab, ...)` are disposed by the scope.

`Dispose()` runs in this order: it cancels `LifetimeToken` (which ends token-bound async work and
disposes every `AddTo(scope)` registration), disposes the child scopes installed by sub-container
exports, disposes the scoped instances, and then disposes the singletons and other owned providers in
reverse registration order. Async work therefore stops before the services it uses are torn down. In
a scene, the context calls `Dispose()` from `OnDestroy`.

The canonical `HealthService` from [Getting Started](../Getting-Started.md) shows all three
attachments in one class: `damage.Subscribe(OnDamaged).AddTo(scope)`, `RegenerateAsync(m_scope.Token)`,
and a `ReactiveProperty<int>` the scope created with `BindReactiveProperty`.

## Lifetimes

| Lifetime | Instances | Disposed by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `AsSingle()` | one per declaring scope, shared with its children | the declaring scope |
| `AsScoped()` | one per resolving scope, built with that scope's dependencies | the resolving scope |
| `AsTransient()` | a new instance per resolve | nobody; the caller owns it |

A child container inherits the parent's bindings. A binding declared on the child shadows the parent's
binding only inside the child. An `AsScoped()` binding declared on the parent gives each resolving child
its own instance:

```csharp
using Onity.DI;                 // OnityContainer

using OnityContainer parent = new OnityContainer();
parent.Bind<IClock>().To<GameClock>().AsSingle();
parent.Bind<IMatchState>().To<MatchState>().AsScoped();
parent.Build();

using OnityContainer child = new OnityContainer(parent);
child.Bind<IClock>().To<ReplayClock>().AsSingle();     // shadows IClock in the child only
child.Build();

// child.Resolve<IClock>()       -> ReplayClock
// parent.Resolve<IClock>()      -> GameClock
// child.Resolve<IMatchState>()  -> one child-owned MatchState on repeated calls
// parent.Resolve<IMatchState>() -> a separate parent-owned MatchState
```

Disposing the child disposes its own singletons and scoped instances and cancels its own token; it does
not dispose the parent. Disposing the parent cancels the child's token too, because the tokens are
linked.

Mapping from VContainer:

| VContainer | Onity |
| --- | --- |
| `Lifetime.Singleton` on the root scope | `AsSingle()` on the root container |
| `Lifetime.Scoped` | `AsScoped()`; resolve through the child scope that should own the instance |
| `Lifetime.Transient` | `AsTransient()` |

## Scope lifetime token

Every container has a lifetime token: `OnityContainer.LifetimeToken` is a `CancellationToken` that
`Dispose()` cancels first, before it disposes child scopes, scoped instances and singletons. The token
source is created on the first request, so a container whose token is never requested allocates nothing
for it.

| Member | Namespace | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `OnityContainer.LifetimeToken` | `Onity.DI` | Canceled when the container is disposed; a disposed container returns a canceled token. A child's token is linked to its parent's, so disposing the parent cancels the child's token too. |
| `IOnityScopeLifetime` (`Token`, `IsDisposed`) | `Onity.DI` | The scope as an injectable contract. `OnityContainer` implements it, and every Unity context binds it to its own container, so a service that injects it receives the scope that owns it. |
| `disposable.AddTo(scope)` | `Onity.DI` | Disposes the `IDisposable` when the scope ends, immediately if it already ended. The scope keeps the disposable until then, so dispose short-lived subscriptions yourself. |
| `OnityContext.LifetimeToken` | `Onity.Unity.Contexts` | The context's container token, canceled when the context is destroyed or its scene unloads. Before `Awake` creates the container it is the context's destroy token. |
| `component.GetScopeCancellationToken()` | `Onity.Unity.Async` | The `LifetimeToken` of the nearest `OnityContext` on the component's GameObject or its parents; without one, the component's destroy token. Main thread only; cache the result instead of calling it every frame. |

A service that subscribes and runs a loop for the life of its scope:

```csharp
using System.Threading;
using Onity.DI;                 // IOnityInitializable, IOnityScopeLifetime, AddTo(scope)
using Onity.Messaging;          // IMessageBroker, Subscribe<T>
using Onity.Unity.Async;        // OnityTask, OnityTaskVoid

public sealed class RespawnTimer : IOnityInitializable
{
    private const float k_respawnSeconds = 5f;

    private readonly IOnityScopeLifetime m_scope;

    public RespawnTimer(IOnityScopeLifetime scope, IMessageBroker broker)
    {
        m_scope = scope;
        broker.Subscribe<PlayerDied>(OnPlayerDied).AddTo(scope);   // unsubscribed when the scope ends
    }

    public void Initialize()
    {
        RunAsync(m_scope.Token).Forget();                         // canceled when the owning context is destroyed
    }

    private async OnityTaskVoid RunAsync(CancellationToken token)
    {
        while (!token.IsCancellationRequested)
        {
            await OnityTask.Delay(k_respawnSeconds, token);
            // Respawn work.
        }
    }

    private void OnPlayerDied(PlayerDied message)
    {
        // Start the countdown.
    }
}
```

Outside a Unity context, bind the scope yourself with `container.BindInstance<IOnityScopeLifetime>(container)`
or pass `container.LifetimeToken` directly. Async build callbacks receive the scope token automatically;
see [Build and async startup](dependency-injection.md#build-and-async-startup).

## Disposal ownership

`Dispose()` disposes the scope's singletons, scoped instances and installed child scopes. Who owns
what:

- Objects the container constructed (`AsSingle()`, `AsScoped()`): the scope disposes them when they
  implement `IDisposable`.
- Objects the binding helpers created: the scope owns and disposes them. This covers the primitives of
  `BindReactiveProperty`, `BindSubject`, `DeclareMessage`, `DeclareAsyncMessage` and
  `BindAsyncReactiveProperty`, and the prefab pool of `BindPooledFactory(prefab, ...)`. Disposing that
  pool destroys its inactive clones; instances still checked out stay with their owners, and a later
  `Release` into it throws `ObjectDisposedException`.
- Objects you pass to `BindInstance`: caller-owned. The container does not dispose them. The same holds
  for a pool you build and pass to `BindPooledFactory(pool)`; tie it to the scope with
  `pool.AddTo(container)` when the scope should dispose it. See
  [Pool lifetime](factories-and-pooling.md#pool-lifetime).
- Transient instances: caller-owned.

In a scene the context disposes its container in `OnDestroy`, so you rarely call `Dispose()` by hand.

## The automatic lifecycle

Implement a lifecycle interface (`Onity.DI`) on a singleton, a scoped binding or a bound instance,
bind the type, and the owning container collects it at `Build()`. There is no separate entry-point
registration. Transient bindings are not collected, because there is no single instance to drive.
Child scopes installed by `FromSubContainerResolve` run their own build and receive ticks from the
requesting scope.

| Interface | Method | When it runs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `IOnityInitializable` | `Initialize()` | once, at the end of `Build()`, in binding-registration order; every dependency is resolvable |
| `IOnityAsyncInitializable` | `InitializeAsync(CancellationToken)` | once, in `BuildAsync()` after the async build callbacks, one at a time in binding-registration order; a context runs it from `Start` and becomes ready after it completes |
| `IOnityTickable` | `Tick()` | once per frame, from the context's `Update` |
| `IOnityFixedTickable` | `FixedTick()` | once per physics step, from the context's `FixedUpdate` |
| `IOnityLateTickable` | `LateTick()` | once per frame after all `Tick()` work, from the context's `LateUpdate` |

```csharp
using Onity.DI;                 // IOnityInitializable, IOnityTickable
using Onity.Messaging;          // IPublisher<T>

public sealed class WaveDirector : IOnityInitializable, IOnityTickable
{
    private readonly IPublisher<WaveStarted> m_waves;

    public WaveDirector(IPublisher<WaveStarted> waves)
    {
        m_waves = waves;
    }

    public void Initialize()
    {
        m_waves.Publish(new WaveStarted(1));   // runs once after Build(); dependencies are ready
    }

    public void Tick()
    {
        // Runs every frame while the owning context is alive.
    }
}
```

Binding it is the whole wiring (fragment): `container.BindInterfacesAndSelfTo<WaveDirector>().AsSingle();`.
`BindInterfacesAndSelfTo` binds the lifecycle interfaces along with the concrete type, so one instance
is both injectable and driven. Lifecycle singletons are created at `Build()`; other singletons stay
lazy. A rebound tickable stops the old instance and starts the replacement. Outside a Unity context,
drive the ticks yourself with `container.Tick()`, `FixedTick()` and `LateTick()`; `Build()` runs
`Initialize()`, and `await container.BuildAsync()` runs `InitializeAsync()`.

For per-frame work in a `MonoBehaviour`, subscribe to `OnityUnityObservable.EveryUpdate()`
(`Onity.Unity.Reactive`) and retain it with `TakeUntilDisable(this)`; see [Reactive](reactive.md). A
bound service ticks through `IOnityTickable`, which costs no subscription.

## Async initialization

`IOnityAsyncInitializable` is the awaitable startup interface. The container collects it like
`IOnityInitializable` and awaits it in `BuildAsync`:

```csharp
using System.Threading;
using System.Threading.Tasks;
using Onity.DI;                 // IOnityAsyncInitializable
using Onity.Unity.Async;        // OnityTask

public sealed class SaveLoader : IOnityAsyncInitializable
{
    private readonly ISaveStore m_store;

    public SaveLoader(ISaveStore store)
    {
        m_store = store;
    }

    public async ValueTask InitializeAsync(CancellationToken cancellationToken)
    {
        await m_store.LoadAsync(cancellationToken);      // canceled when the scope is destroyed first
        await OnityTask.NextFrame(cancellationToken);    // OnityTask awaits work here too
    }
}
```

- Order: `Build()` (sync callbacks and `Initialize()`), then the async build callbacks, then each async
  initializer one at a time in binding-registration order.
- Thread: each callback and initializer starts on the context the build started on, the main thread in
  a Unity context, even when the previous one completed on a worker thread.
- Token: the scope's `LifetimeToken`, linked with the `BuildAsync` caller's token when one is passed.
  Destroying the context mid-initialization cancels it, leaves `IsReady` false and cancels `ReadyTask`
  without logging an error.
- Failure and retry: a fault ends `BuildAsync` and the context logs it. The next `BuildAsync()` call
  resumes at the first initializer that has not completed; completed initializers do not run again. An
  initializer bound after a completed `BuildAsync` runs on the next call.
- Readiness: `OnityContext.IsReady`, `ReadyTask` (a BCL `Task`) and `WaitReadyAsync(cancellationToken)`
  (an `OnityTask` that resumes on the main thread) all cover the async initializers. The token passed
  to `WaitReadyAsync` cancels that wait only; the build keeps running.

## Unity contexts

A context (`Onity.Unity.Contexts`) is a `MonoBehaviour` that owns one container. In `Awake` it creates
the container (with the discovered parent context's container as parent), binds the defaults, runs the
installers in its Installers list, calls `Build()`, and, when Auto Inject Hierarchy is on, member-injects
every `MonoBehaviour` under its own GameObject that is not owned by a nearer context. In `Start` it runs
`BuildAsync(LifetimeToken)`. `Update`, `FixedUpdate` and `LateUpdate` pump the ticks. `OnDestroy`
disposes the container, which cancels the scope token first. Destroying a context while its async build
runs cancels the build without logging an error and leaves `ReadyTask` canceled.

Every context binds: the container, `IResolver`, `IOnityScopeLifetime` (the container), the context
itself, `MessageBroker` with its interfaces, and `OnityEventHub`. That is why a
service can inject `OnityEventHub`, `IMessageBroker` or `IOnityScopeLifetime` with no installer line;
see [Events and Messaging](events-messaging.md).

| Context | Role | Execution order | Parent discovery |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ProjectContext` | Global root that persists across scene loads; `ProjectContext.Instance`, `DontDestroyOnLoad` | `-10000` | none |
| `SceneContext` | One scope per scene | `-9800` | the Project Context field, else `ProjectContext.Instance` |
| `GameObjectContext` | One scope per prefab or object subtree | `-9700` | the nearest `OnityContext` above it in the hierarchy, else `ProjectContext.Instance` |

Serialized fields:

| Field | On | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Installers | every context | empty | the `MonoInstaller` components run in order during `Awake` |
| Parent Context | every context | none | an explicit parent; leave empty for automatic discovery |
| Auto Inject Hierarchy | every context | on | member-inject the MonoBehaviours under the root in `Awake`; installers and contexts are skipped |
| Run Async Build Callbacks | every context | on | run `BuildAsync()` in `Start`; when off, `Start` marks the context ready without running anything async |
| Project Context | `SceneContext` | none | an explicit `ProjectContext`; leave empty to use `ProjectContext.Instance` |
| Find Parent In Hierarchy | `GameObjectContext` | on | search the parent hierarchy for the nearest context |
| Fallback To Project Context | `GameObjectContext` | on | use `ProjectContext.Instance` when no parent context is found |

Add a context by searching its name (for example `Scene Context`) in Add Component; there is no Onity
submenu. A context's `InjectGameObject(root)` injects objects you instantiate at runtime under it.

## Where each installer goes

The context decides a service's lifetime, so put each installer on the context whose lifetime matches
the service:

- Project-scope services go in an installer on the `ProjectContext` prefab: anything that must live for
  the whole session and survive scene loads, such as settings, saves, currency, inventory, audio and
  scene flow.
- Per-scene collaborators go on that scene's `SceneContext`: a match's rules, presentation and spawn
  factories, per-screen controllers. A `SceneContext` is a child of the project context, so a scene
  installer depends on project services without rebinding them.
- Per-object graphs go on a `GameObjectContext` on the prefab root: an enemy's brain and its parts, a
  UI panel and its presenters.
- Never put a project-scope installer on a `SceneContext`. The scene scope is rebuilt on every scene
  load, so its singletons do not persist.

`ProjectContext` is loaded before the first scene by `ProjectContextBootstrap`, a
`RuntimeInitializeOnLoadMethod` that runs before scene load and instantiates the prefab at
`Resources/Onity/ProjectContext` when no `ProjectContext` exists yet. Create that prefab once with the
menu `Onity/Contexts/Create ProjectContext Prefab`, which saves it at
`Assets/Resources/Onity/ProjectContext.prefab`, then add the project installers to its Installers list.
A `SceneContext` finds `ProjectContext.Instance` on its own, or through its Project Context field.

```text
ProjectContext (Assets/Resources/Onity/ProjectContext.prefab)
    Installers: [ProjectInstaller]                 // persists across scenes
SceneContext
    Installers: [GameInstaller]                    // per scene; resolves the project services above
```

## Scene transitions

`Onity.Unity.SceneFlow` can hide a scene change behind a screen cover and can keep the next scene built
in the background. Both outlive the scene that asks for them, so bind them on the `ProjectContext`:

```csharp
public sealed class SceneFlowInstaller : MonoInstaller
{
    [SerializeField] private OnityScreenFadeView m_fade;   // on the ProjectContext prefab

    public override void InstallBindings(OnityContainer container)
    {
        container.BindInstance<IOnitySceneCover>(m_fade);
        container.Bind<IOnitySceneReadiness>().To<OnityActiveSceneReadiness>().AsSingle();
        container.BindInterfacesAndSelfTo<OnityCoveredSceneTransition>().AsSingle();
        container.BindInterfacesAndSelfTo<OnityScenePreloader>().AsSingle();
    }
}
```

`OnityCoveredSceneTransition.RunAsync(change, showCover, token)` shows the cover, runs the change, waits
until the new active scene's `SceneContext.ReadyTask` completes (plus the settle frames of
`OnitySceneRevealPolicy`, with a maximum wait), then hides the cover. With `showCover: false` the same
flow runs with no cover; `RunAsync(change, cover, token)` uses another cover for one change, and a null
cover means none. The change receives the transition's own lifetime token, because the scene that asks is
usually the one the change unloads; the caller's token ends only the caller's wait. One change runs at a
time: a request while another runs, or after disposal, returns `false` at once. A change that throws hides
the cover over the old scene again and fails the task with its exception.

```csharp
bool ran = await m_transition.RunAsync(
    token => OnitySceneFlow.TransitionAsync(m_profile, OnitySceneFlowStateId.Gameplay, request, token),
    showCover: true,
    cancellationToken);
```

Covers are `IOnitySceneCover` implementations. `OnitySceneCoverView` is the base for a cover drawn by
one element of a `UIDocument`: it owns the timing (unscaled, a serialized duration and curve each way), the
cancellation, input blocking and hiding, and a derived cover only implements `ApplyProgress(progress)`
(0 is clear, 1 is covered). Two ship with templates under `Runtime/Unity/UI/SceneFlow`:

- `OnityScreenFadeView` with `OnityScreenFade.uxml`: fades the USS color (black), or its optional
  image. Give each image its own fade view and pass the one you want to `RunAsync`.
- `OnityIrisCoverView` with `OnityIrisCover.uxml`: a circle wipe drawn with `Painter2D`, closing on its
  `Center` (normalized panel position).

Put the cover's `UIDocument` on the `ProjectContext` prefab with a `PanelSettings` whose sort order is
above every other panel. A visible cover blocks presses below it; a clear one is `display: none`. The
animation allocates nothing per frame.

`OnityScenePreloader` keeps one scene ready: `PrepareAsync(sceneName, prepareData, token)` loads it
additively behind the active scene, and `TryStartAsync(sceneName, startData, token)` starts it in one
frame (it becomes active, the old scene hides with `OnitySceneVisuals.Hide` and unloads). The prepared
scene learns it is being prepared from `OnityScenePreloader.TryGetPrepareData<T>(gameObject.scene, out T)`
while it installs, keeps itself hidden, and binds an `IOnityPreparedScene` that decides which start
requests it accepts (`CanStart`) and shows itself in `Activate`. Prepare data is kept per loading scene,
never in the shared `OnitySceneTransitionStore` slot, so a scene-flow transition running at the same time
cannot take it. `TryStartAsync` returns `false` when nothing matching is prepared; load the scene normally
then. The preloader knows nothing about covers, so the two compose in the change:

```csharp
await m_transition.RunAsync(async token =>
{
    if (await m_preloader.TryStartAsync("Game", request, token) == false)
    {
        await OnitySceneFlow.TransitionAsync(m_profile, OnitySceneFlowStateId.Gameplay, request, token);
    }
}, showCover: useCover, cancellationToken);
```

`OnitySceneScopes.TryFind(scene, out SceneContext context)` finds a loaded scene's context; call it once
per scene change, never per frame.
